q: Pink-skinned and heavily perfumed, one Peloponnese variety is pressed carefully to keep its wine white, and a cool plateau in Arcadia is its home. Name the grape.
exp: Mantinia is the designation, sitting at around six hundred and fifty metres, and the wine is low in alcohol, sharp and floral, with rose petal and citrus peel. The skins carry enough colour that a longer maceration turns the wine pink, which is bottled at regional level rather than under the designation.

q: Robola vines on Cephalonia grow straight out of bare limestone scree, and the Venetians who ruled the island left a nickname recording it. What did they call the wine?
exp: Vino di sasso is the phrase, and the vineyards sit on rubble steep enough that every part of the work is done by hand. Robola gives a dry white with a lemon and crushed-stone character and a faintly waxy weight, and it is grown seriously almost nowhere else.

q: Black laurel is what the name of one grape means, and the sweet fortified red of Patras is built on it. Name the grape.
exp: The wine is fortified during fermentation and then aged oxidatively in cask, frequently by blending across vintages, so it arrives tasting of raisin, coffee and dried fig. A handful of producers make a dry red from the same grape, which is a very different and much rarer thing to meet on a list.

q: A fortified rock town in the southeastern Peloponnese shipped sweet wine across medieval Europe and left its name on a family of grapes still grown from Italy to Madeira. Name the town.
exp: Malvasia is the name in its travelled form, and much of what the town shipped was probably gathered from the islands and merely sold through its harbour rather than grown behind it. A modern designation has revived the link, and the variety called Monemvasia on Paros is one of the family carrying the name home.

q: A nineteenth-century formula for Chianti allowed a white grape so the wine would drink well young. Which white was named?
exp: Bettino Ricasoli set out Sangiovese with Canaiolo for structure and a little Malvasia for early appeal in 1872. He treated the white share as optional, but the 1967 DOC made it compulsory at ten to thirty percent, 1996 made it optional again, and from the 2006 vintage white grapes were banned from Chianti Classico outright.

q: Flaky, friable marl that splits into plates underlies many of the best sites between Florence and Siena. What is that soil called locally?
exp: Galestro breaks up easily and drains hard, which suits Sangiovese on a slope. Alberese, a hard compact limestone, is the other rock name worth knowing in the same hills.

q: Cooler, higher ground in the Sieve valley northeast of Florence gives the Chianti subzone most often singled out for longevity. Which subzone is it?
exp: Altitude and a cool draught out of the Apennines slow ripening and hold acidity. The wines start tighter and reward cellaring more than most Chianti does.

q: Since the 2006 vintage a whole category of grape has been shut out of the Classico blend. Which category?
exp: Trebbiano and Malvasia had been permitted for over a century and were often used to stretch volume. Removing them was the single clearest step in Classico's move upmarket.

q: A Classico producer wants the denomination's top tier, which demands estate-grown fruit and thirty months of ageing. Which designation is that?
exp: Introduced in 2013 above Riserva, and unusual in tying the tier to fruit the estate farmed itself. Riserva by contrast can be built from bought grapes.

q: Outside the Classico zone the Sangiovese minimum sits at seventy percent. Inside it, what does the rulebook demand?
exp: The remaining fifth may be Canaiolo, Colorino or an international variety, and many estates now bottle the wine as pure Sangiovese anyway. The wider Chianti DOCG stays at seventy.

q: Some producers restart a finished wine with dried, part-raisined grapes to build body and softness. What is that Tuscan practice called?
exp: The renewed fermentation adds a little alcohol and glycerol and rounds off hard young tannin. It fell out of favour with the drive for concentration and has been revived by growers chasing drinkability.

q: West of Florence a small DOCG has required Cabernet in its blend since long before anyone spoke of Super Tuscans. Name it.
exp: The rules oblige at least a tenth Cabernet Franc or Sauvignon alongside Sangiovese. Cabernet was growing there under the name uva francesca in Medici times, which makes the zone the oldest precedent for what Bolgheri later made famous.

q: Ferruccio Biondi-Santi propagated a particular Sangiovese selection in the nineteenth century. What is that selection called locally?
exp: Brunello means little dark one and refers to the fruit rather than the wine. Prugnolo Gentile, Morellino and Nielluccio are the same grape's names in Montepulciano, the Maremma and Corsica.

q: A Montalcino estate declassifies younger fruit into a wine it can sell a year after harvest. Which denomination takes it?
exp: Rosso is the same grape from the same hill under a much shorter ageing requirement, which lets an estate protect the Brunello in a difficult year. It is often the better value and always the earlier drink.

q: Shelter from an extinct volcanic cone keeps this zone drier and warmer than the Chianti hills to its north. Which peak gives that shelter?
exp: Amiata breaks up storms coming off the Tyrrhenian, so Montalcino sees markedly less rain than Chianti Classico. Growers there worry about drought where growers further north worry about rot.

q: An estate in Montalcino plants Cabernet and Chardonnay alongside its Sangiovese. Under which local DOC may it bottle them?
exp: Sant'Antimo is the catch-all denomination covering everything on the hill that is not Brunello, Rosso or Moscadello. It is named for the Romanesque abbey below the town.
